newsitem.title: JAPAN: New Asia-Pacific finance forum may be mostly talk.
newsitem.headline: New Asia-Pacific finance forum may be mostly talk.

text.p: Media were quick to dub a new forum for discussions among six Asian-Pacific economies the "Group of Six", but officials seem keen to play down any expectations that it will yield much more than talk at first.

Analysts were equally wary of predicting any bold new steps when senior central bank and finance ministry officials from the United States, Japan, China, Hong Kong, Singapore and Australia meet in Tokyo on Tuesday to discuss economic policy and financial market matters.

"This is going to be the first meeting of this kind, so I really wonder whether any concrete results would come out, although there are topics of common concern," said C.H. Kwan, a senior economist at Nomura Research Institute.

Finance officials from the world's seven leading industrial nations -- the United States, Japan, Germany, France, Britain, Italy and Canada -- meet regularly as the Group of Seven (G7) to coordinate economic policies. G7 leaders gather once a year to mull mutual economic and political concerns.
Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said this week that he hoped the new forum would meet on a regular basis and in future be upgraded to include finance ministers and central bank chiefs.
Others, however, were quick to seek to scuttle comparisons with the G7. "This is a meeting, not a group," U.S. Deputy Treasury Secretary Larry Summers told reporters on Thursday.

Former Japanese vice finance minister Makoto Utsumi echoed that view. "I don't think it will function like the G7 to discuss specific issues and so on, but is a kind of forum for more dense discussion," he said earlier this week.

Among the topics seen on the agenda are ways to improve cooperation in financial markets, macroeconomic policies, financial industry supervision and possible responses in the event of an Asian version of the Mexican financial crisis.
Finance and monetary authorities from the Asia-Pacific region already gather regularly under a variety of umbrellas.
Finance ministers from the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum meet annually, as do APEC leaders.

Last year, the meeting of the 11-member EMEAP (Executive Meeting of East Asia and Pacific Central Banks), set up at the Bank of Japan's initiative to further regional central bank ties, was upgraded to the central bank chief level. Southeast Asian central bank governors from 10 nations also meet yearly.

Japanese officials stressed the importance of having both China, a growing economic powerhouse, and the United States, whose currency dominates the region, in the new and smaller forum, and analysts said Hong Kong was keen to be involved ahead of its return to Chinese sovereignty later this year.

"The major currency in the Asian region is the U.S. dollar, so it's meaningful for the United States to participate," a senior official of Japan's Finance Ministry said. "China has the second largest foreign reserves after Japan and it is still increasing its reserves. Chinese participation is essential."

Regional foreign exchange stability is another likely topic of discussion. But analysts said next week's talks were unlikely to be directly linked to any expansion of existing regional pacts aimed at stabilising local currencies.

In a landmark step last April, Japan's Finance Ministry and the Bank of Japan entered into dollar-based repurchase pacts with seven Asia-Pacific central banks to provide each other liquidity in times of currency crisis. Some Japanese officials have also floated the notion of yen-based repurchase pacts.
Washington, however, has shown no interest in becoming involved in the existing repurchase arrangements.

"To make the repo pacts any more formal than where we are today would start smacking of something like the Nyborg agreements, which were the foundations for the ERM (Exchange Rate Mechanism)" said Angus Armstrong, chief economist for Asia-Pacific at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Singapore.

Armstrong added that a more likely outcome next week was the establishment of a dialogue "where they consider what the regional objectives are and what methods could be used if there's a requirement to stabilise some of the regional markets".
